1:
The verse marks a hinge in the Gospel and four of them say so in nearly the same words. Bede states it structurally: up to this point Mark has related what our Lord said and did in Galilee, and here he begins what he did and suffered in Judaea, first across Jordan on the east and afterwards on this side, at Jericho, Bethany and Jerusalem. He adds a geographical caution, that although the whole province is generally called Judaea to distinguish it from other nations, the name belongs more especially to its southern portion, as against Samaria, Galilee and Decapolis. Ellicott places the seam by the harmonists, who insert a long stretch of Matthew, most of Luke’s central section and a large part of John between the ninth chapter and this one, and takes the farther side of Jordan for the Peraean ministry. Robertson makes the same point with arithmetic attached: a full third of Luke’s Gospel has intervened, and where the close of the ninth chapter stood six months from the end, this stands weeks from it. He traces the route, north through Samaria and Galilee, across Jordan into Peraea and back into Judaea near Jericho, and reads the crowds as caravans of passover pilgrims travelling with Jesus rather than merely meeting him, which is how Ellicott takes the verb too, literally to journey together. Clarke notes that many transactions fall between the two chapters which Matthew and Mark omit and Luke and John supply, and offers a point on the opening verb, that it may be rendered he departed thence, a sense the purest Greek writers give it. Lightfoot presses the chronology hardest. Here, he says, is need of a discerning eye to distinguish the true time and method of the story, since half a year or thereabouts comes between the words just before and this journey, though the evangelists seem to intimate that he set out as soon as he had finished speaking; in fact he had gone up to Jerusalem through Samaria for one feast, returned to Galilee, gone up again for another, and only then come beyond Jordan. His conclusion is about how the Gospels are made: God so directed the pens of these writers that some omitted what others were to supply, so that a full history is composed only out of them together.

Why he went to that region and no further is Theophylact’s question. He enters Judaea, whose envy had often driven him out, because his Passion was to take place there; but he does not go up to Jerusalem yet, keeping to the confines so that he might do good to multitudes who were not evil, since Jerusalem was, through the malice of its leaders, the worker of all the wickedness. Bede sets the two groups against each other in the same way: the multitude gather to be taught and to have their sick healed, while the Pharisees come only to try whether they can deceive their Saviour by tempting him. Gill and Wesley both place the departure from Galilee, Gill naming Capernaum.

Henry takes the verse as a portrait of Christ’s working habits. He was an itinerant preacher who did not stay long in a place, since the whole land was his parish, so that he would visit every part and instruct its remotest corners; his circuit was like the sun’s, from whose light and heat nothing is hid. Wherever he came he did as he was wont, preaching; preaching was his constant work. Henry also compares the accounts: where Matthew says he healed them, Mark says he taught them, the cures confirming the doctrine and the doctrine explaining the cures. And he fastens on the word again, drawing from it that even those whom Christ has taught need teaching again, both because the fulness of Christian doctrine leaves more to learn and because we are so forgetful.
2:
What the Pharisees were after is agreed on and then specified differently. Gill says simply that they came as they came everywhere, not to be instructed but to ensnare. Theophylact describes the shape of the trap: they proposed a question with a precipice on either side, so that whether he answered that a man might put away his wife or that he might not, they could accuse him and contradict him out of the doctrines of Moses; and Christ, being Very Wisdom, answers without falling into either. Robertson weighs the participle, granting that the word can mean testing rather than tempting and that one commentator takes it so here, but holding that their motive was evil in any case. He offers two guesses at the specific hope. They had once entangled the Baptist with Herod Antipas and Herodias on exactly this subject and may have wanted the same result again; or they may have been probing whether Jesus would prove stricter than Moses, since they knew he had already spoken on divorce in Galilee.

The counter-question, and the order in which the two sides raise Moses, is where Augustine does his work. Matthew has the Pharisees produce the bill of divorcement after our Lord has forbidden separation, whereas Mark has them produce it in answer to a question of his; and Augustine holds that this makes nothing to the truth of the fact. Christ’s wish was to give them no account of why Moses permitted it until they had mentioned the permission themselves, and since the intention of the speakers, which is what words are meant to express, is shown either way, there is no discrepancy though there is a difference in the manner of relating. He offers a second harmonisation as well: the question What did Moses command? may itself have been the reply to men who had already asked his opinion about putting away a wife, so that when they answered that Moses permitted a bill, he replied about that same law and how God instituted marriage, on hearing which they returned to their first point and asked why Moses commanded it at all. Robertson reads the same exchange as a deliberate move behind the concession: Jesus at once raises what Moses taught, and then goes back past that concession to the state commanded at the creation.

On the bill itself Robertson supplies the philology and the party politics. The word is a diminutive, a little book, which an early English version rendered a libel of forsaking; and the fact that the Pharisees press this point suggests they held the liberal position of one rabbinic school, allowing easy divorce for almost any cause, which he notes was the popular view then as now, while Jesus takes the stricter position of the rival school. Gill marks the joints of the dialogue — that Christ answered very prudently and wisely, that they replied by way of rejoinder, and that his next word bears specifically on the command, or rather the sufferance, of Moses which they had urged.

What the hardness of your heart concedes is read two ways. Chrysostom takes the clause as a rescue and a reversal: by it Christ saves Moses, who had given the law, from their accusation, and turns the whole charge upon their own heads. Pseudo-Chrysostom reads it as a statement about what marriage requires of a person: a soul purged of desire and of anger is able to bear the worst of women, but where those passions have a redoubled force over the mind, many evils arise out of hatred in marriage — so that the permission measures the men it was given to.
6:
Chrysostom builds the argument out of the order of creation. Christ brings the discourse back to the old law by going behind Moses to the beginning; and if he had wished one wife to be put away and another brought in, he would have created several women. Nor did God merely join one woman to one man, he also bade the man quit his parents and cleave to his wife, and the very word cleave shows the impossibility of severing a marriage, since two framed out of one root will join into one body. Then, Chrysostom notes, comes an awful argument: Christ did not say do not divide, but concluded that what God has joined man must not put asunder — from which he infers that if two persons God has joined may not be separated, much more is it wrong to separate from Christ the Church God has joined to him.

Wesley reads the same phrase for what it settles elsewhere. Because Christ says from the beginning of the creation, Moses in the first chapter of Genesis must be giving an account from that beginning, and Wesley asks whether it does not follow that there was no creation previous to the one Moses describes. From the second clause he draws a second conclusion, that Adam did not at first contain both sexes in himself but was made male only and Eve female only, the two being joined in a state of innocence as husband and wife. Gill works on the wording rather than the doctrine, noting that from the beginning of the creation of the world is a form of speech the Jews used often, and that the words of the creation are absent from two versions and from the oldest copy known to him, which reads simply from the beginning; at the next verse he flags a Persian addition of brethren and sisters with no foundation in the passage cited or in any copy of the evangelist.

That the disciples raise the matter privately is a detail two of them mark as peculiar to this Gospel. Ellicott observes that Mark’s narrative is on the whole much shorter than Matthew’s, and yet the question coming from the disciples inside the house is given by him alone. Pseudo-Jerome explains the word again in the same verse: the second question is said to be asked again because it concerns the subject the Pharisees had raised, and the remark is made by Mark in his own person. Gloss takes the repetition as a lesson in itself, that a saying of the Word repeated produces not weariness but thirst and hunger, since they that eat wisdom shall yet be hungry and they that drink her shall yet be thirsty; and it is on that account that the Lord instructs his disciples over again.

On the saying itself Robertson notes what Mark omits: the exception clause that stands in Matthew is absent here, though he judges the point really involved in what Mark does record, since a merely formal divorce does not annul a marriage actually consummated, while the breaking of that bond does. Wesley draws a different consequence in five words, that all polygamy is here totally condemned. Pseudo-Chrysostom explains why the second union is called adultery at all: the name belongs to cohabitation with one who is not a man’s wife, and she is not his wife whom he has taken after quitting the first, so that the adultery is committed upon the second woman he brings in. He adds that the law forbade what was plainly adultery, whereas the Saviour forbids this, which was neither plain nor known to all though contrary to nature; and he settles a harmonising question in passing, that Matthew reporting these words to the Pharisees and Mark to the disciples involves no contradiction, since he may have spoken them to both.
12:
That a wife could divorce a husband at all is the question the verse raises, and the three who take it up give three different answers. Gill denies it outright as Jewish practice: there was no such law and no such sufferance under Moses for a woman to put away her husband as there was for a husband to put away his wife, nor was it done among the Jews, unless it had come into use about this time in their declining state, borrowed from the Gentiles. Clarke reads the verse the other way, that from this it appears the wife did in some cases assume the very same right — while admitting in the same breath that he can find no such right recorded anywhere in the Jewish laws. He then argues for the arrangement on principle: a law giving the permission all on one side would be unjust and oppressive, whereas when it is equally balanced and the right is the same on each side it serves as a mutual check and prevents the very evils it was meant to cure; and he notes that several instances occur of Jewish women taking other men during their husbands’ lifetime without any law being found under which they were punished. Robertson settles the historical point by distinguishing law from practice: Greek and Roman law allowed a wife to divorce her husband where Jewish law made no provision for it, but the thing was nonetheless done, as in the case of Herodias and of Herod’s sister Salome. He then rejects the inference two commentators draw from that — that Mark added the clause to the words of Jesus for the benefit of the Gentile readers of a Roman Gospel — on the ground that Jesus knew perfectly well the thing was done in the Roman world and had reason to prohibit it.

Ellicott marks what is distinctive about the verse rather than what lies behind it. This clause too is peculiar to Mark, and it is the only place in our Lord’s teaching that states the case of the wife who divorces her husband and marries again and passes sentence on her, alongside the husband who divorces his wife and the wife who is so divorced. All three cases, he says, are dealt with on the same two grounds: that the marriage relationship ought to be indissoluble and that one cause only justifies or permits its dissolution, and that any further permission of divorce is merely a concession to the hardness of men’s hearts for the avoidance of greater evils.

On what should follow from all this, Clarke and Ellicott are plainly at odds. Ellicott allows exactly one cause, and treats every wider permission as a concession made to hard hearts rather than a right. Clarke lays down a rule of his own that is not drawn from the text at all: divorce should never be permitted except on the ground that the parties are miserable together and are both perfectly willing to be separated — and where that holds and everything else is proper, he would have them go different ways, so that they do not ruin both themselves and their hapless children.
13:
Theophylact sets the scene by contrast: the wickedness of the Pharisees has just been related, and now the great faith of the multitude appears, who believed Christ conferred a blessing by the mere laying on of his hands. Robertson notes that the verb for bringing is an imperfect implying repetition, that the children were of various ages, and that the mothers wanted him to touch them; he quotes the remark that the incident follows with singular fitness on our Lord’s assertion of the sanctity of married life, and adds an aside about what is not in view, that no question of baptism or salvation was involved, this being simply a natural thing to do. Gill identifies the bringers as the parents, friends or nurses of children in those parts, who had heard his fame and held him a great prophet, and carried the children in their arms. Barnes explains the request itself, that to touch them means to lay hands on them and pray for them, it being common to lay hands on the head of a person for whom a blessing was asked, as Jacob did. Henry presses what the request implies about those who made it. The children needed no bodily cure and were not yet capable of being taught, so those who had the care of them must have been concerned chiefly about their souls, which he takes for the principal care every parent owes a child; and they must have believed Christ’s blessing would do those souls good, knowing he could reach their hearts when nothing a parent said would reach them. He also reads the episode as an encouragement not only to children to come to Christ young but to grown people conscious of their own weakness.

Why the disciples interfered, and how the rebuke lands, is treated by all of them. Chrysostom is charitable about the motive: they forbade the bringers out of regard for the dignity of Christ; and our Saviour, to teach them modesty and to tread worldly pride underfoot, takes the children to himself and assigns them the kingdom of God. Origen, whose comment the compiler has run into the same paragraph, turns it into a rule for teachers. If any who hold the office of teaching in the Church should see someone bringing them the foolish of this world, the low born and weak — called children and infants for that reason — let him not forbid the man who offers such a one to the Saviour; and let disciples already grown to full stature condescend to be useful to children, becoming as children to gain them, since he himself, being in the form of God, humbled himself and became a child.

On the displeasure the moderns work at the word and its force. Ellicott notes that the term, as used of our Lord, is peculiar to this Gospel, Matthew applying it only to the disciples and to the chief priests. Robertson parses it as an ingressive aorist, that he became indignant, and calls it a strong word of deep emotion; and he presses the application hard, that it ought to be a joy to parents to bring their children to Jesus and certainly to let them come, so that to hinder them is a crime, and some parents will answer to God for keeping their children away. Barnes gives two reasons for the indignation: it was a pleasure to Christ to receive and bless little children, and the disciples were doing what they had never been told to do, interfering where it was plainly improper. Wesley makes the same points more briefly, that they blamed people who were not blameworthy and tried to hinder children from a blessing, and reads the saying that follows as meaning the members of the kingdom Christ came to set up are such as these, grown persons of a child-like temper included.
15: What receiving the kingdom as a child means is answered by each in his own terms and they do not quite coincide. Ellicott notes first that Matthew omits the verse and Mark shares it with Luke, then defines it as receiving the kingdom after the manner of a child, with simplicity and faith, humility and love; and he applies it against the disciples themselves, since men disputing which of them was greatest in the kingdom were as if they had not even entered it. Barnes lists the qualities: teachable, mild, humble, free from prejudice and obstinacy — and he presses the negative clause hard, that whoever does not receive it so shall not be a real member of the family of Christ on earth, though he may be a professor, and shall never enter heaven. Bede offers two readings. Either the innocence and purity of a child’s mind is what is required, or else the point lies in how a child is taught: he does not contradict his teachers or muster reasonings and words against them, but receives with faith what they teach and obeys with awe, and so we are to receive the word of the Lord with simple obedience and no gainsaying. Robertson lands in the same place from a different direction, that a little child learns to obey its parents simply and uncomplainingly, and this trusting and loving obedience is the model set before adults; he adds a remark on the psychology of his own day, that some who argue against teaching children obedience have produced results which have not been inspiring. He also enters a caution the others do not: Jesus does not here say that children are in the kingdom because they are children. Wesley gives the shortest definition of all, receiving it as one who totally disclaims all worthiness and fitness, as if he were but a week old; and Gill notes that the opening formula is the one our Lord used when about to assert something of moment and importance, which he would have attended to. Theophylact, commenting a verse earlier on the same saying, presses the wording of the phrase before it: Christ says not that the kingdom belongs to these but to such, meaning those who have in their intention and their work the harmlessness and simplicity that children have by nature. A child does not hate and does nothing of evil intent; though beaten he does not quit his mother, and though she clothe him in vile garments he prefers them to kingly apparel — and just so, the man who lives by the good ways of his mother the Church honours nothing above her, not even pleasure, which is the queen of many.
16:
On the embrace itself the descriptions are careful. Ellicott prefers folded them in his arms and leaves open whether they were lifted from the ground at all, noting that the word is Mark’s alone and that the blessing, though implied in Matthew, is stated only here. Robertson reads the gesture as a distinct rebuke to the over-particular disciples, finds a repeated action in the imperfect and a hand laid on each child in the participle, and calls it a great moment for every mother and child there. Gill collects the versions, which have him take them upon his arms or into his bosom, all expressing great tenderness. Pseudo-Chrysostom reads the same action theologically: he lifts them into his own bosom as one reconciling himself to a creation that had fallen from him and been separated from him, and he lays his hands on them as other men are wont to do, though his operation is not as theirs, since being God he kept to human ways of acting as being very man. Bede finds in the embrace the same lesson as in the saying, that the lowly in spirit are the ones worthy of his blessing and grace.

Two of them turn the blessing directly into an argument for infant baptism, and one has already ruled it out. Barnes frames it as a question of privilege rather than duty: the question for a parent is not whether he ought to present his children by prayer but whether he may, and so with baptism, not whether he ought to devote them in that ordinance but whether he may do it — an inestimable privilege, not a matter of stern and iron-handed duty. Clarke argues from the embrace itself: if Christ embraced them, why should not his Church embrace them, and why not dedicate them to God by baptism, whether by sprinkling, washing or immersion, since the mode need not be disputed. He then turns on those who withhold it in terms sharper than anything else in the chapter, calling it grossly heathenish and barbarous in parents who profess to believe in a Christ who loves children, noting that such people are ready enough to send for a minister when they think the child at the point of death, and adding that it would be no crime to pray they might never hear the words my father or my mother from their own child’s lips. Robertson, commenting on the same scene a few verses earlier, had already said that no question of baptism or salvation was involved in it at all.
17:
The approach itself is read closely, and Mark’s two details are what draw the comment. Robertson notes that Jesus had left the house and was proceeding with the caravan when the ruler ran up and knelt and was asking — the running and the kneeling both peculiar to this Gospel. Henry treats the manner as a series of favourable signs. He came running, which shows humility, since he laid aside the grandeur of a ruler, and earnestness, as one in haste for the conversation; he came when Christ was in the way and in company, not insisting on a private interview by night as another ruler had done; and he knelt, in token of the veneration he had for a teacher come from God, as one meaning not merely to do obeisance then but to obey always. Barnes reads the running the same way, as the intensity of a man who wanted to know the way of life, adding that such zeal is proper and cannot be too intense if well directed. Lightfoot works on the kneeling, which the versions render variously, and suspects more is meant than they convey: those who did such reverence customarily took hold of the knees and kissed them, and he gathers rabbinic instances, including a wife who kissed her husband’s knees after twelve years apart. Gill supplies the movement between the scenes, that after blessing the children Christ left the coasts of Judea and turned toward Jerusalem. Bede supplies the connection of thought: the man had just heard that only those willing to be like little children may enter the kingdom, and wanted it explained to him openly rather than in parables by what works a man might attain everlasting life.

The counter-question is where the doctrinal weight falls, and each of them guards it differently. Bede refuses to let it be read as a disclaimer. By the one good God we must understand not only the Father but the Son, who calls himself the good Shepherd, and the Holy Ghost, since the Father gives the good Spirit to those who ask — the undivided Trinity being the one and only good God; so the Lord does not deny that he is good but implies that he is God, and does not deny that he is a good Master but declares that no master is good save God. Chrysostom explains the reply by the questioner’s assumption: the man had come to Christ as he would to a man, and to one of the Jewish teachers, and Christ answered him as Man — which does not exclude men from goodness altogether but only from comparison with the goodness of God. Theophylact makes it a deliberate lift: the Lord meant to raise the young man’s mind so that he might know him to be God, and at the same time to teach that in conversing with a man one should not flatter him but look back to God, the fount of goodness, and give the honour there. Robertson states the modern form of the same guard, that the language is not a disclaiming of deity on the part of Jesus, and reads the question as a challenge to the ruler to define what he meant by the word — whether he was using it in the absolute sense that belongs to God. Ellicott says the same in different terms, that the drift of the question was to force the man back on the conditions of absolute goodness and make him ask how far, and on what terms, the word could be used of any child of man at all. Theophylact registers his surprise at the enquirer too: where everyone else comes to Christ to be healed of some infirmity, this man asks for everlasting life — and asks it, as the end of the story shows, while loving his money.
19:
That the answer should point to the commandments at all is explained by Bede from the economy of the law: the righteousness of the law, kept in its own time, conferred not only earthly goods but eternal life on those who chose it, and so a man asking about everlasting life is properly told that he knows the commandments. Gill adds what could be assumed of the questioner, that the Jews taught these to their children, so that he might reasonably be expected to know what they were and how many — though, Gill judges, he was ignorant of their extent and their spirituality.

The clause that draws the attention is the one Mark alone supplies. Ellicott marks defraud not as peculiar to this Gospel and reads it as a special application of the tenth commandment, aimed at this man in particular: one who had great possessions gathered in the usual ways by which men get wealth needed to examine himself by that text above all others. He presses it as a series of questions — were there no ill-gotten gains in his treasure, had no wages of the reaper been kept back, had no sharp bargains been driven with widows or orphans or the poor? Barnes reaches the same clause from the other side, defining fraud as taking away a neighbour’s property by dishonesty and noting that to cheat presupposes a covetous desire and is commonly attended by falsehood or false witness in getting it; so the single prohibition condenses the ninth and tenth commandments together, and he observes that it stands in those terms in Leviticus.

On the reply the tone is caught differently. Gill hears a great deal of pertness in it. Robertson notes only the emphatic form of the words, these all of them. Wesley catches something the others pass over, that the man now stands reproved and quietly drops the epithet he had begun with, addressing him simply as Master and no longer as good. Bede also notes which commandments are chosen, the second table rather than the first, so that the enquiry about eternal life is answered from the duties a man owes his neighbour; and Gill observes that these are the commands God gave to Moses on Sinai, so that the appeal is to a body of law the questioner had known since childhood rather than to anything new.
21:
The look and the love are Mark’s alone, and the commentators divide over how much to make of them. Robertson says plainly that Jesus fell in love with the youth. Clarke gives three grounds, his youth, his earnestness and his sincerity; Wesley one, the dawnings of good Christ saw in his heart. Barnes is the most careful to limit it: the sequel showed the young man no true disciple, so the word denotes natural affection, or that Jesus was pleased with his amiableness and outward regard for the law — consistent with deep sorrow that he would not give his heart to God. Gill draws the line more sharply, distinguishing the special love with which Christ loves those given him by the Father from a human affection for whatever moral good appeared; and he reads the look as an unspoken correction, since Christ could not believe the commandments perfectly kept yet declined to reproach the man with a lie. Origen and Pseudo-Chrysostom go the other way. Origen takes the gesture as an endorsement, since in loving him Christ appears to affirm the truth of his profession, having seen that he answered with a good conscience. Pseudo-Chrysostom raises the difficulty directly — how could he love a man he knew would not follow? — and answers that the love earned by keeping the law was not forfeited merely by failing to reach perfection. Lightfoot and Ellicott independently supply the gesture from custom, Lightfoot gathering rabbinic instances of a teacher rising to kiss the head of a pupil who had spoken well, Ellicott suggesting a steadfast look and perhaps a kiss on the brow.

What the one lacking thing is gets four answers that are not quite the same. Barnes reads the command as a test of sincerity: sell, and see whether you love God more than wealth. Clarke names the lack as a heart disengaged from the world, and rules out the alternatives sharply — to say it was something else, when Christ explains his own meaning here, is to be wise above what is written. Wesley calls it the love of God, without which all religion is a dead carcass, and names the obstacle as his great idol. Calvin denies that the one thing lies outside the law at all. The law nowhere obliges anyone to sell everything, but since it represses sinful desire and teaches readiness for hunger and poverty, a man still burning with covetousness is far from keeping it; and Christ names one thing because he need not preach to him about fornication or murder but only lay a finger on the sore.

On what is to be done with the money Calvin is most exact. Christ enjoins not merely the selling but the giving, since parting with riches would not of itself be a virtue but a vain ambition; and he instances the philosopher applauded for throwing his money into the sea, when it would have been better to bestow it on others — so what Christ applauds is not the bare surrender but liberality in relieving others. Cyril of Jerusalem presses the same point furthest: gold and silver are not, as some think, the devil’s, since God says by the prophet that they are his, and a man who has used a good thing badly and will not blame his own management impiously throws the blame on the Creator. A man may even be justified by money, since the meat given to the hungry came from it, and money may become a door of the kingdom on the very terms named here. Ellicott adds that the call to take up the cross is peculiar to Mark, showing with what clear prevision our Lord looked to the manner of his own death; Calvin makes that clause the heaviest part of the demand, a man accustomed to ease being told to put his shoulders under a cross.
22: The two who work on the word find the same picture in it. Ellicott prefers he frowned to the received rendering, noting that the verb is the one translated lowering of a threatening sky elsewhere in the Gospels; Robertson traces it to an adjective meaning sombre or gloomy and says the man’s face darkened like a lowering cloud, remarking that the word is rare enough to appear only twice in the Greek Old Testament and once in a classical historian. Gill lists what the man had been asked to bear, that he lacked one thing, that he was to sell all he had and give it away, and — what may have weighed as heavily — that he was to take up a cross of reproach and persecution; his countenance fell on all of it together. Clarke does not analyse the word at all but pronounces on the man: this young man had perhaps been a saint, and an eminent apostle, had he been poor. From that he draws the general lesson, that it is oftentimes a misfortune to be rich — and closes with the two questions that give the remark its edge, who is aware of this, and who believes it.
23:
Mark’s glance is again what draws notice. Ellicott says the look and gesture are mentioned by this evangelist alone; Robertson calls it another picture of the looks of Jesus and quotes two judgments on it, that the glance was to see what impression the incident had made on the Twelve and that when the man was gone the Lord’s eye swept round the circle as he drew them the lesson. Gill reads the same purpose into it, that Christ looked to see what effect the conversation had produced and to gather their attention to what he was about to say. Robertson notes at the next verse why blank astonishment was the response: the disciples, in common with other Jews, regarded wealth as a token of God’s special favour. Gill puts the expectation concretely, that they looked for the kingdom of the Messiah to be set up in worldly pomp, with the rich men of the nation coming into it and supporting its splendour.

The address to them as children is felt by three as a softening. Barnes takes it for an expression of affection, though perhaps also a reproof, since their slowness to understand was childlike and the saying had to be repeated. Robertson finds the tender note due to their growing perplexity and observes that Christ addresses the Twelve so nowhere else. Wesley admires the manner of it, that he softens the harsh truth by the way he delivers it and yet without retracting or abating one tittle.

The words Wesley then expounds are precisely the words two others regard as no part of the text. Ellicott notes that for them that trust in riches has the appearance of limiting and so softening the sternness of the previous utterance, and holds that there is good reason to think it added by someone seeking to tone the warning down to what seemed a rational medium, since the best manuscripts lack it; omit the doubtful words, he says, and the sentence reads simply how hard it is to enter into the kingdom of God — hard for rich and poor alike, though hardest for the rich, as what follows shows. Robertson reports the same evidence and the same verdict, listing the witnesses that omit the phrase and noting that a modern critical text drops it as an evident addition made to explain a difficult saying. Wesley builds his whole exposition on the clause, taking the trust to mean reliance on riches for defence, or happiness, or deliverance from the thousand dangers to which life is exposed; that such men cannot enter the kingdom he calls clear and undeniable, and he draws the conclusion that gives the saying its force — it is easier for a camel to go through a needle’s eye than for a man to have riches and not trust in them, and therefore easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom.
25: On the camel and the needle Robertson supplies the vocabulary, that each evangelist uses a different word for the perforation, Mark’s coming from a verb meaning to wear away or bore through and Luke’s being the surgical needle; and at the close he uses the saying about God to sweep away a familiar evasion, since the impossible beside men becomes possible beside God, and that is the whole point, brushing aside all petty theories of a gate called the needle’s eye. Barnes glosses the disciples’ second astonishment as meaning no more than exceedingly, and Gill explains why it increased, since the comparison seemed to them to make it not merely hard but utterly impossible for a rich man to be saved, so that they asked one another who then could be saved at all. Robertson notes that the connective in their question carries an inferential force, as though they were drawing the conclusion out loud. Gill reads the final look as Christ seeing both by their countenances and by his own omniscience what they were reasoning privately among themselves. Henry gathers the lesson for both conditions at once. Those who eagerly seek the wealth of the world will never rightly prize Christ and his grace; and on the other side there is the greatness of the salvation of those who have little of this world and leave even that for Christ, the sharpest trial of a good man’s constancy being when love to Jesus calls him to give up love to friends and relatives. So we are to learn contentment in a low state and to watch against the love of riches in a high one, praying to be enabled to part with all if it is required and to use in Christ’s service all that we are allowed to keep. Theophylact offers two possibilities for the camel itself, either the animal or else the thick cable used on large vessels, and reads the closing saying as turning on where a man stands: when we listen to God the thing becomes possible, but so long as we keep our human notions it stays impossible. Christ does not call riches bad, he adds, but calls those bad who have them only to watch over them carefully, teaching us not to keep and preserve them but to spend them on what is needed.
28:
Why Peter speaks when he does is explained the same way by everyone. Gloss connects it directly to the man who has just walked away: the disciples had already fulfilled the precept the youth could not bear to hear, and so began to ask about their reward, thinking they had done a great thing, since one who had kept the commandments of the law could not hear the further demand without sadness. Gill has Peter recovering from the astonishment of the previous saying and taking heart, then offering their own case as an instance of it, since the power that made them quit their small substance could also work the same effect on the heart of a man ever so rich. Robertson says it was hard for Peter to hold in till now, notes that Matthew has him answering as though the remark had been addressed to him in particular, and reads the whole speech as a claim of obedience to the high ideal, in contrast with the conduct of the rich ruler. Theophylact enters a qualification about the scale of it: Peter had left few things, and yet calls them his all, for even a few things hold us by the bond of affection, so that a man who leaves a little is blessed. Bede adds what he takes to be the decisive half of Peter’s claim, that leaving all is not sufficient by itself and the perfection lies in the words that follow, and have followed thee; the question then amounts to saying that they have done what was commanded, and asking what the reward will be.

The answer is read as deliberately wider than the question. Theophylact notes that Peter asks only about the disciples while our Lord answers generally, and then guards the promise against a plain misreading: Christ does not mean that we should leave our fathers without helping them or separate ourselves from our wives, but instructs us to prefer the glory of God to the things of this world. He works the point out from the apostles’ own case, that many women busied themselves about their food and clothing and ministered to them, and that they had many who loved them as fathers and mothers, so that Peter, having left one house, afterwards had the houses of all the disciples. Chrysostom hears something else under the same words, a covert announcement that persecutions were coming, since many fathers would allure their sons to impiety and many wives their husbands; and he takes the two forms of the clause together, that Mark has for my sake and the Gospel’s where Luke has for the kingdom of God, since the name of Christ is the power of the Gospel and of his kingdom, the Gospel being received in that name and the kingdom coming by it. Ellicott notes what Mark leaves out at this point, the special promise that the Twelve should sit on thrones judging the tribes of Israel, and suggests he may have omitted it as writing for Gentile converts. Gill marks the same omission without offering a reason. Clarke reports a variant in the clause about the Gospel, preferring the reading for the sake of on the authority of a long list of manuscripts and nearly all the versions.
30:
Whether the hundredfold is literal or figurative is the question, and it divides them sharply. Barnes says flatly that it cannot be taken literally, as promising a hundred times as many mothers and sisters; it means the loss is a hundred times compensated, so that in religion a man has a hundred times the value of everything he forsook — the pardon of sin, the favour of God, peace of conscience, support in trial and in death, and new friends raised up in the room of those left behind. He adds that godliness profits the present life too, since obedience secures industry, temperance, prudence, health and the confidence of the world. Pseudo-Chrysostom had settled it the same way in one sentence: the reward must be in participation and not in possession, since the Lord fulfilled it to them spiritually and not carnally. Clarke resists exactly that move. Some, he says, in flat opposition to the text, have made the promises wholly spiritual; and while he grants that those who leave all do find among genuine Christians spiritual relations as dear to them as fathers and mothers, he insists the hundredfold is often literally fulfilled, since wherever a Christian travels among Christians the shelter of their houses and the produce of their lands are at his service so far as he needs them — and he notes that the words were spoken first to disciples whose life was itinerant. He reads the phrase as in this very time, and takes the promise as one of providence, that though Jews and Gentiles conspired against them nothing would be lacking while anything was necessary. Wesley threads between the two: not in the same kind, since it will generally be with persecutions, but in value, a hundredfold more happiness than any or all of those things could afford — adding that none is entitled to this happiness but the man who will accept it with persecutions. Gill puts the same distinction more briefly, that the promise is not of a hundred houses or brethren but of enjoying in this present life what is a hundred times better than any of the things named.

Bede uses the verse against a school of interpreters rather than for a doctrine. Some, he says, take occasion from the promise of a hundredfold in this present time to teach the doctrine of a thousand years after the resurrection of the just, when everything left for the Lord’s sake is to be restored with manifold usury besides the crown of everlasting life. His objection is that the promise so understood exposes itself: in the hundred wives which the other evangelists mention its foulness is made manifest, particularly when the Lord testifies that there is no marriage in the resurrection, and when he says that what is put away for his sake is received again in this life with persecutions — which on their own account will not occur during those thousand years. Robertson notices the same detail from the other end, recording the observation that Jesus omits a hundred wives from the list, which he says leaves a well-known imperial sneer on that score without foundation.

The clause about persecutions is Mark’s alone and both who mark it read it biographically. Ellicott suggests it may have been engraved on Peter’s mind by his own experience, since he had learned to see in the fiery trial almost the necessary condition of the exceeding joy. Robertson allows that the language borrows from familiar descriptions of the blessings of the Messianic kingdom while holding that Jesus uses such idiom only to idealise it, and observes that the apostles were soon to see this foreshadowing of persecution realised. Clarke notes that a long list of manuscripts and versions adds fathers to the things restored.
32:
The picture of Christ walking ahead is what everyone stops at. Robertson reads the grammar for the scene: the imperfect describes the disciples’ feelings while Jesus was walking on in front of them, an unusual circumstance in itself that seemed to bode no good, and those who followed were afraid as they watched him going ahead in solitude — the idiom, he notes, may mean not all of them but only some. He quotes the judgment that the Lord walked in advance with a solemnity and determination which foreboded danger, and adds that they read the face of Jesus correctly. Henry makes the same detail an emblem of command: Jesus went before them as the captain of our salvation, now to be made perfect through sufferings, showing himself forward to go on with his undertaking at the very point where it grew hardest, so that when the time was at hand he pressed forward rather than drew back. The disciples, he says, had begun to consider what danger they were running into and how malicious the council at Jerusalem was, and were ready to tremble at the thought; and to hearten them Christ went before them — from which Henry draws the note that when we see ourselves entering on sufferings it is encouraging to see our Master go first. Barnes reads the leading in the same way, as an intrepid guide exposing himself to danger rather than his followers, and locates their amazement precisely: they were afraid harm would come to him in the city, and their fear increased when he told them what would happen, since they were astonished that knowing so well what awaited him he should still persevere in going. Wesley says their amazement was at his courage and intrepidity, considering the treatment he had told them he would meet with, and that their fear was both for him and for themselves.

Bede supplies the reason for the amazement from what had gone before: the disciples remembered the discourse in which the Lord had foretold that he must suffer many things from the chief priests and scribes, and so were amazed at his going up to Jerusalem at all — either lest they should perish with him, or at least lest he whose life and ministry was their joy should fall into his enemies’ hands. He then explains the second half of the verse as a remedy: foreseeing that his Passion would trouble their minds, the Lord foretells to them both the pain of the Passion and the glory of the Resurrection. Theophylact gives a different and stronger reason for the walking in front. It was to show that he runs to meet his Passion and does not refuse death for the sake of our salvation; and the forewarning was to confirm their hearts, so that having heard beforehand they might bear it better afterwards and not be alarmed at its suddenness. He then turns the foreknowledge into an argument: a man who foreknows a danger and does not fly from it, though flight is in his power, plainly gives himself up to suffering of his own will. He adds that Christ takes the Twelve apart because it was fitting that the mystery of the Passion should be revealed to those most closely connected with him, and that he enumerates each thing that was to happen lest, by passing anything over, he should leave them troubled at seeing it come suddenly. Clarke contributes a small point of translation, that the conjunction opening the next clause is better rendered for, which he says gives the reason of the wonder and the fear: they were amazed because he began to tell them on the way what was to befall him. Gill marks only the geography, that they had left the coasts of Judea beyond Jordan and were now on the road.
33:
Gloss works through the prediction clause by clause and glosses each. The Son of man means he to whom suffering belongs, since the Godhead cannot suffer; shall be delivered means by Judas, to the chief priests and the scribes; they shall condemn him means judging him guilty of death; and shall deliver him to the Gentiles means to Pilate the Gentile, and it is his soldiers who mock and spit upon and scourge and put him to death. Gill follows the same division at the next verse, identifying the mockers and scourgers as the Roman soldiers, the one at their governor’s connivance and the other by his order. Ellicott notes a small point of agreement among the Gospels, that the spitting is reported here and by Luke but not by Matthew.

Why the Resurrection is added at the end is Chrysostom’s question, and he answers it from the disciples’ state of mind: so that when they were saddened on account of the Passion and the death they should at the same moment be looking for the rising; and since he had not hidden from them the sorrows and the insults that were coming, it was fitting that they should believe him on the other point as well. Cyril of Jerusalem takes the same prediction as evidence of willingness rather than of foresight merely. Others, who do not foreknow their death, die unwillingly; but he spoke beforehand of his Passion, saying Behold, the Son of man is betrayed to be crucified, and elsewhere it is written that he steadfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem. Cyril then asks why one who could see it coming did not shun it, and answers that it was lest the whole world should perish in its sins — and he presses further, that the Cross is not merely endured but is a glory to Jesus, arguing it from the case of the man who had just risen from the table and drunk the cup of blessing and went out to sell righteous blood, so that hands lately receiving the blessed gifts were plotting a death for the wages of betrayal.
35:
Why the request comes at this moment is agreed. Chrysostom says the disciples, hearing Christ speak often of his kingdom, supposed it was to arrive before his death, and now that his death had been foretold they came to be made worthy of its honours at once. Theophylact puts the same thing more concretely, that they thought he was going up to Jerusalem to reign there and only afterwards to suffer what he had foretold, and it was with those thoughts that they asked for the two places. Robertson notes the dramatic present tense and the bluntness of the wish, and observes that they try to commit Jesus to their desires before saying what those desires are, just like spoiled children; he also identifies the expectation exactly, a grand world empire with apocalyptic features, a dream that brushed aside everything Jesus had said about his death and resurrection as mere pessimism.

Who actually spoke is the one point of difficulty, and it is settled by everyone in nearly the same way. Augustine states it as a harmonisation: Matthew has the words spoken not by the brothers but by their mother, since she brought their wishes to the Lord, and Mark, by implying that they used the words themselves, is speaking briefly rather than differently — and both evangelists agree in having the Lord answer the sons rather than the mother. Clarke reconstructs the scene to the same effect: the mother introduced them and made the request as though from herself, and Jesus, knowing where it came from, addressed himself immediately to James and John, who were standing by, so that the mother is no further concerned in the business. Barnes says simply that they did not come in person but got their mother to make the request; Wesley is blunter still, that it was she and not they who uttered the words; and Gill has the mother as their mouth, speaking for them while they spoke by her, and at the next verses has Christ answering both her and them, and them seconding her motion. Robertson notes that Matthew adds she came worshipping. Chrysostom offers two motives for bringing her at all and allows both: they were ashamed of the human weakness they felt and so took Christ apart from the rest, and, seeing themselves honoured above the others, they thought the petition easily obtained and brought their mother so that she might pray along with them. He also reads the counter-question as deliberate, since Christ asked not from ignorance of what they wanted but from a wish to make them say it themselves.

What they were asking for is measured against what it would mean. Theophylact has Christ answering that it will not be as they think, that he is to reign as a temporal king in Jerusalem, and that the things belonging to his kingdom are beyond their understanding, since to sit at his right hand is so great a thing that it surpasses the angelic orders. Clarke notes that three manuscripts read in the kingdom of thy glory, a kingdom they expected to be set up on earth, and reports a variant conjunction in the following verse supported by a long list of witnesses. Robertson observes that where Mark has in thy glory Matthew has in thy kingdom.
38:
What the cup and the baptism stand for is agreed, which is worth noting because neither figure is obvious. Theophylact says both mean the cross, the cup as a potion sweetly received and the baptism as the cause of our cleansing, and adds that the brothers answered without understanding, supposing he meant a visible cup and the washings the Jews used before meals. Wesley divides the two rather than merging them, the cup for inward and the baptism for outward sufferings, our Lord being filled with the one within and covered with the other without; and he glosses the rebuke as telling them that what they asked for was suffering, which must pave the way to glory. Robertson traces both figures elsewhere, since Jesus calls his death the cup in Gethsemane and had already used baptism as a figure of it, a usage Paul takes up more than once; and Matthew has only the cup where Mark has both. Ellicott presses that into a textual conclusion: the baptism clause seems to have stood originally in Mark alone and to have been added later by copyists of Matthew to bring the two reports into agreement, the best manuscripts of Matthew omitting it twice.

On the confident answer the comment is severe. Gill calls it a second instance of their ignorance, since they knew neither the state whose places they had asked for nor themselves; they were unacquainted with their own weakness as much as with the greatness of what Christ was to endure, and had they understood either they would not have answered so, without a word of the grace of God or any dependence on his strength. He notes too that the previous verse was an answer of a kind, not granting what they wanted but pointing out their ignorance. Bede takes the same line on the request, that those who ask a seat of glory they do not yet merit know not what they ask.

Bede then raises the difficulty the promise creates and answers it from history. How did the two drink the cup of martyrdom, when Scripture relates only that James was beheaded by Herod while John died a natural death? The ecclesiastical histories, he says, record that John too was cast into a cauldron of burning oil for his witness and sent straight from it to Patmos, so that the spirit of martyrdom was in him and he drank the cup of confession — the cup the three children drank in the furnace, though the persecutor never spilt their blood.

What the refusal of the two places actually refuses divides them. Ellicott, dropping the words the translators supplied, reads the clause as saying the seats are not his to give but belong to those for whom they were prepared, and draws the limit exactly: our Lord disclaims not the power of giving but the power of giving arbitrarily, otherwise than his Father willed. Bede reads the refusal as aimed at a disposition, that it is not his to give to proud men such as they were then showing themselves. Gill grounds it in election: there are no such places in the sense petitioned for, the glories of the heavenly state were not to be settled then because they were settled already, and Christ gives them only to those given him by his Father and ordained to that happiness. Wesley grounds the same clause in the opposite place, that the prepared inheritance belongs to those who by patient continuance in well doing seek for glory and honour and immortality, and that he will give every man his own reward according to his own labour. Clarke notes that a variant conjunction is read here by a long list of witnesses, and Robertson, looking ahead to the ransom saying, observes that the apostles did not understand those words when spoken and that they reach us through Peter and Mark.
41:
Theophylact is unsparing about why the ten were angry. Being influenced by human feelings they were moved with envy, and their displeasure arose specifically from seeing that they had not been taken up by the Lord themselves; before that moment they had not been displeased, because they saw themselves honoured above other men. At this time, he says, the apostles were still thus imperfect, though afterwards they yielded the chief place to one another. He then describes the cure as coming in two movements: first Christ draws them to himself in order to comfort them, and then he shows them that usurping honour and desiring the first place belongs to Gentiles, whose great ones thrust themselves into the chief place tyrannically and as lords. Gill notes what it was they had heard, the request made by the sons of Zebedee or by their mother for them, and at the calling adds that they were at some little distance yet near enough for Christ to discern the heat and passion they were in, knowing that they had the same ambitious views as the two brothers.

On the wording of the contrast Ellicott twice notices that the form is indicative rather than imperative: the sentence reads that whoever will be great among them shall be their minister and shall be servant of all, not that he is to be told to become so. Gill records a variant that turns the opening clause into a command, and reports one version’s rendering that it ought not to be so among them — such a lordly spirit not becoming them, being heathenish. Ellicott also refers the two verbs used of the Gentile rulers to the fuller discussion of their force in the parallel Gospel.

Bede states the principle and then the example. He teaches that the greater is the one who is less and that the man who is servant of all becomes lord; so it was vain both for the two to seek immoderate things and for the ten to be annoyed at their seeking them, since the height of virtue is reached not by power but by humility. Then Christ proposes an example, that if they thought lightly of his words his deeds might shame them — he came not to be ministered unto but to minister and to give his life a ransom for many. On those last two words Bede presses a limit: he did not say that he gave his life a ransom for all, but for many, meaning those who would believe on him. Wesley reads the identical phrase in the opposite direction, that the ransom was for as many souls as needed such a ransom. Gill treats the clause as the last step of the argument, that to everything already urged Christ adds his own example, to teach his disciples humility and lowliness of mind and to check their ambitious desires.
46:
How many blind men there were is the first question, and it gets two different answers. Bede states the problem plainly: Matthew has two sitting by the wayside, and Luke has one enlightened with a like order of circumstances as Christ was going into Jericho; but no wise man will suppose the evangelists wrote things contrary to one another, only that one wrote more fully what another left out, and that one of the two was the more important, as appears from Mark giving his name and his father’s. Augustine agrees on why Mark singles him out — his receiving sight had won the miracle a fame proportioned to how widely his affliction was known — but parts company on Luke: although Luke relates a miracle done in entirely the same way, we must understand that a similar miracle was wrought on another blind man by a similar method. Barnes takes the simplest line, that Matthew says there were two and Mark mentions only one without denying the other, naming him because he was well known. Henry disposes of it in a sentence, that if there were two there was one, and then turns to the name: some take it to mean the son of a blind man, so that he was the blind son of a blind father, which made the case worse and the cure more wonderful, and the fitter to typify the spiritual cures Christ’s grace works on those who are not only born blind but born of those that are blind.

The name itself is worked over by three. Lightfoot reports the charge that the evangelist commits a tautology in translating a Syriac word that needed no translating, since no evangelist writes Bartholomew, the son of Tholomeus. He grants the observation and answers it twice: when the second element is a common noun rather than a proper name it is not ill-sounding to interpret it, as with the sons of thunder and the son of consolation; and the phrase may be rendered otherwise than the son of Timaeus, either a son of admiration or, more properly, a son of profit, a sense he finds in the Targum. Clarke gives the plain derivation, that the Syriac word means son and the father’s name was Timeus, notes that some suppose the explanatory clause an interpolation, and holds that the man is named because he was the most remarkable of the group. Robertson compares the formation with Bartholomew, observes that Mark alone gives the name, and adds the topography, that the old and the new Jericho are distinct, the Roman town lying about five miles west of Jordan and fifteen east of Jerusalem. He renders the crowd as considerable rather than merely great, notes that all three Gospels picture the man sitting by the roadside as a common sight, and remarks that Bartimaeus had his regular place. Gill supplies the movement through the town, and Henry the social point, that those whom providence has disabled from getting a livelihood by their own labour are the most proper objects of charity.

Two of them read the place-name allegorically. Jerome says the name of the city agrees with the approaching Passion, since Jericho means moon, or anathema, while the failing of the flesh of Christ is the preparation of the heavenly Jerusalem. Bede takes the same etymology to a different point, that Jericho meaning the moon indicates the waning of our fleeting race. Pseudo-Chrysostom explains where the beggar got his title for Christ: he calls him Son of David because he heard how the passing multitude praised him and felt sure that the expectation of the prophets was fulfilled.
49:
Everything Mark alone reports in these verses is noticed. Ellicott says the better manuscripts give the more vivid and said, Call him, and that the cheering words of the bystanders belong to this Gospel only, as does the man’s casting off his outer mantle and leaping up — the Greek there being much stronger than the English rose. Robertson confirms the picture from the tenses, an ingressive participle for the standing still and vivid dramatic presents through the exchange, and calls the message that Christ was calling him joyful news. Barnes and Clarke and Wesley all fasten on the discarded garment. Barnes takes it for the loose outer robe, thrown off in joy at the prospect of healing and so that he might run unimpeded, and then uses it as an illustration — though granting the verse had no such original reference — of how a sinner should come to Christ, throwing away the garments of his own righteousness. Clarke describes the garment as the blanket or loose cloth that was the usual upper covering of an Asiatic mendicant and his protection from the weather, and draws the same lesson more sharply: if every penitent were as ready to throw aside his self-righteousness and sinful encumbrances as this man was to throw aside his cloak, there would be fewer delays in conversions than there are. Wesley compresses it into three words, that he did it through joy and eagerness. Gill notes the garment was little worth in any case and that he threw it off to make quicker despatch.

On the address the man uses, Ellicott and Robertson both prefer the Aramaic form over the translation. Ellicott says the word is not simply Lord but the augmentative of Rabbi, expressing greater reverence, and occurring in only one other passage in the New Testament; he takes it as a further instance of Mark’s fondness for reproducing the very syllables that were spoken. Robertson agrees on the form and adds two things: that the verb rendered receive my sight means to see again, so that the man had apparently once been able to see, and that giving sight to the blind was among the things expected of the Messiah.

The fathers read the exchange for what it teaches about prayer. Bede asks whether one able to restore sight could be ignorant of what a blind man wanted, and answers that the question is put so that prayer may be made to him, to stir up the blind man’s heart; and he observes that a blind man looks down on every gift except light, since whatever he may possess he cannot see it without light. Chrysostom gives a second reason for the question, that no one should think what was granted was other than what the man wanted, since it was Christ’s practice to make the good disposition of those about to be cured known to everyone before applying the remedy, both to stir up others to emulation and to show that the man was worthy to obtain the grace. Origen reads the rebuke of the crowd against the man rather than for him: those who went before and were foremost in believing charged him to be silent and to stop calling Christ by what they took for a contemptible name, when he ought to have said Son of God; and Origen observes that this blind man is the greater of the two, since Luke’s was not called but had to be brought, as though unable to come himself.
52: On the closing word about faith the readings run from the plain to the doctrinal. Robertson notes that the verb commonly means save and that this may be the sense here, and finds in the imperfect a picture of Bartimaeus following the caravan into the new Jericho. Ellicott infers that he went up with the company to Jerusalem and suggests his prominence in Mark implies he became known in the Church afterwards, his new sight qualifying him as an eyewitness of the week that followed. Calvin takes the word furthest: by faith is meant not merely a confident hope of recovering sight but the conviction that Jesus was the promised Messiah, and not a confused knowledge either, since the confession was drawn from the Law and the Prophets, so that the man did not bestow the title at random but embraced the person whose coming the predictions had taught him to expect. He then presses the general rule, that though God’s power sometimes extends even to unbelievers, no one enjoys his benefits rightly unless he receives them by faith, and that the word here is not limited to an outward cure but includes the soul. Theophylact ends where the narrative does, that the man’s mind was grateful, since when he was made whole he did not leave Jesus but followed him — and followed him in the way, that is, in this life, after which all are excluded who do not follow him here by working his commandments. Gill glosses the dismissal itself, noting that one version reads it as see rather than go thy way, and taking the phrase to mean that the request is granted and the man may go home and about his business. Clarke reports a variant in the last clause, preferring the pronoun to the repeated name on the authority of a long list of witnesses, since the name had occurred immediately before and repeating it would be neither necessary nor elegant. He closes on the character of the miracle, that it shows not only sovereign power but benevolence, and that we never see that power used except in the way of benevolence — asking how slow God is to punish and how prone to spare, and whether it can gratify infinite benevolence to destroy any of the children of men. We must take great heed, he adds, not to attribute to his sovereignty acts inconsistent with his mercy, an error he thinks prevailing and confined to no one religious party.
